series.title: Sherlock Holmes
series.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
series.logline: A brilliant, emotionally armored consulting detective and the steady doctor who chronicles him take on the impossible crimes of Victorian London — and the one adversary clever enough to nearly end them both.
series.note: The canon spans four novels and dozens of short stories; this demo focuses on five foundational books that carry Holmes and Watson from their first meeting through the Moriarty conspiracy and its aftermath. Told almost entirely through Watson's eyes, it is as much a story about friendship and observation as it is about crime.

threads.name: The Moriarty Conspiracy
threads.source: First named directly in "The Final Problem," though its shadow arguably touches every earlier case where Holmes senses an organizing intelligence behind London's crime.

threads.name: The Woman
threads.source: Watson's opening line of "A Scandal in Bohemia" — Irene Adler's single appearance, and the outsized permanent impression it leaves on Holmes.

threads.name: The Agra Treasure
threads.source: A decades-old theft during the Indian Mutiny that resurfaces in London as pearls, a map, and a wooden-legged man with an old debt to collect.

threads.name: The Baskerville Curse
threads.source: A centuries-old family legend of a spectral hound, revived — and manufactured — to clear a path to inheritance.

threads.name: Holmes and Watson's Partnership
threads.source: From a shared advertisement for lodgings in A Study in Scarlet to the deepest friendship in the canon — the throughline underneath every case.

threads.name: The Rivalry with Scotland Yard
threads.source: Holmes's running, good-humored contempt for official police methods, and the Yard's grudging, repeated need for him anyway.

characters.name: Sherlock Holmes
characters.oneLine: The world's first and only consulting detective, a reasoning machine who treats emotion as a contaminant in an otherwise perfect instrument.
characters.source: Sherlock Holmes canon, Arthur Conan Doyle (public domain)

relationships.note: His only real intimacy; Watson is both the one person who can reach him and the one person who documents him to the world.
The one person smarter than Holmes, though too indolent to ever act on it.
The only adversary who ever matched him — an equal and opposite intellect, which is precisely why Holmes cannot let the matter rest.
Long-suffering keeper of 221B, tolerates the chemistry experiments, the revolver practice, and the visitors at all hours.
Scotland Yard's most persistent visitor to Baker Street; exasperated by Holmes, but always comes back for help.
The only person, in Watson's telling, ever to outwit Holmes — and a woman, which unsettles him more than the defeat itself.

links.note: His rooms, his laboratory, his stage.
The throughline that defines the back half of his career as Watson records it.

arcs.want: To prove his deductive method against a real, unsolved case — to be taken seriously by the official police
arcs.need: To find a partner who can witness and translate his gift for an audience that doesn't understand him
arcs.wound: Years of being dismissed as an eccentric obsessive by everyone except his own intellect
arcs.rationale: He drives every event in the investigation and is already formidably skilled, but Watson (and the reader) still see him as a curiosity rather than a person — relatability is the last thing to arrive.

arcs.want: A case difficult enough to hold off the boredom that drives him to cocaine
arcs.need: To reckon with the fact that his methods have a human cost, not just an intellectual payoff
arcs.wound: A mind so fast that ordinary life moves too slowly to bear
arcs.rationale: Slight relatability bump — watching Watson fall for Mary Morstan forces Holmes to notice, briefly, what he's opted out of.

arcs.want: To keep winning — to remain the undefeated reasoning machine
arcs.need: To be shown, once, that intellect isn't the only kind of power in the room
arcs.wound: A pride so total it has never had to survive a real loss
arcs.rationale: Capability peaks here — this is Holmes at his most dazzling across a dozen cases — but "A Scandal in Bohemia" cracks him open just enough that relatability jumps; losing to Irene Adler is the first time he reads as fully human.

arcs.want: To end Moriarty for good, whatever it costs
arcs.need: To accept that some victories require disappearing — that being right isn't the same as being safe
arcs.wound: The horror of discovering his equal exists, and that matching wits with him means matching risks
arcs.rationale: Everything peaks. This is the most proactive and most human Holmes gets in the demo — he chooses Watson's safety over his own pride, which is new for him, and then apparently dies for it.

arcs.want: To debunk the supernatural explanation and expose the human hand behind it
arcs.need: To trust Watson enough to send him ahead alone and stay hidden himself — a real test of the partnership under strain
arcs.wound: Chronologically set before Reichenbach in the story's internal timeline, but read after it — the shadow of his "death" colors how the audience sees every risk he takes here
arcs.rationale: A slight step back from Memoirs' peak — this case is more procedural, but the trust he places in Watson (going undercover on the moor alone) is its own quiet growth.

lessons.trigger: Irene Adler outmaneuvers him and leaves before he can act
lessons.lesson: Intellect alone does not guarantee victory; underestimating an opponent's resourcefulness is itself a failure of observation
lessons.becomes: Slightly less contemptuous of "the softer passions" as a category of intelligence

lessons.trigger: Realizing Moriarty threatens Watson's life, not just his own
lessons.lesson: There are things worth more to him than the game itself
lessons.becomes: Willing to fake his own death rather than risk his friend

characters.name: John Watson
characters.role: Doctor, army veteran, chronicler of Holmes's cases
characters.oneLine: A steady, decent man whose ordinary courage and unfailing loyalty make him the one person Holmes can't out-deduce his way past.
characters.source: Sherlock Holmes canon, Arthur Conan Doyle (public domain)

relationships.note: Meets him as a stranger looking to split rent; becomes the one fixed point in Holmes's life.
His client-turned-love in The Sign of Four; her passing (referenced later in canon) is why he returns to Baker Street lodgings by Hound of the Baskervilles.
Fond, familiar; she trusts Watson to manage Holmes when no one else can.
Watson records Lestrade's grudging respect for Holmes more generously than Holmes himself ever would.

links.note: His home before marriage, and again after.
Nearly loses his closest friend to it, and believes he has, for three years of the internal timeline.

arcs.want: Cheap lodgings and something to occupy a mind bruised by war
arcs.need: A sense of purpose after being invalided out of the army
arcs.wound: The Second Anglo-Afghan War — a wound to his shoulder (or leg, in later inconsistent tellings) and to his nerve
arcs.rationale: He's the reader's entry point — high relatability from page one — but he's a passenger in this case, watching Holmes work rather than driving events himself.

arcs.want: To help solve Miss Morstan's case
arcs.need: To let himself want something for himself again, not just live in service of Holmes's work
arcs.wound: A war widower's loneliness he hasn't admitted to
arcs.rationale: This is Watson's most personal arc in the demo — he gets his own want (Mary) and his own change (marriage) independent of Holmes's case.

arcs.want: To properly chronicle Holmes's genius for the public
arcs.need: To reconcile his admiration for Holmes with his own new domestic life
arcs.wound: The nagging sense that Holmes needs him more than a married man can always provide
arcs.rationale: Capability ticks up slightly — he's a more confident narrator and occasional participant by now — but his role is still primarily witness.

arcs.want: To protect Holmes from Moriarty's reach, even without understanding the whole plan
arcs.need: To grieve — to face losing Holmes and go on recording the truth of him anyway
arcs.wound: Believing, for the writing of this book, that his best friend is dead
arcs.rationale: Relatability peaks — this is the most emotionally exposed Watson gets, writing what he believes is an elegy for his friend.

arcs.want: To handle the Baskerville case competently on his own, since Holmes has sent him ahead alone
arcs.need: To trust his own judgment without Holmes there to confirm it
arcs.wound: Widowed, and thrown back into bachelor lodgings and old habits
arcs.rationale: His highest proactivity and capability in the demo — for much of this book he IS the detective on the ground, and rises to it.

lessons.trigger: Meeting Mary Morstan as her protector
lessons.lesson: He can have a life of his own alongside his loyalty to Holmes, not instead of it
lessons.becomes: A married man who still comes running when Holmes calls

lessons.trigger: Sent to Dartmoor alone, forced to investigate without Holmes's direct guidance
lessons.lesson: His own careful observation, learned from years beside Holmes, is enough to carry a case
lessons.becomes: A capable investigator in his own right, not merely a recorder

characters.name: Professor Moriarty
characters.oneLine: A brilliant former mathematics professor who built and commands the invisible architecture of nearly every organized crime in London — the "Napoleon of crime."
characters.source: Sherlock Holmes canon, Arthur Conan Doyle (public domain)

relationships.note: The only mind Holmes has ever met that matches his own — which is exactly why one of them has to fall.

links.note: Where the conspiracy — and, apparently, both men — meet their end.

arcs.want: To eliminate Holmes, the only threat to his criminal empire
arcs.need: None — he is presented as fully formed, a pure antagonistic force with no interiority Watson is given access to
arcs.wound: Unknown; Doyle deliberately withholds his origin, making him more myth than man
arcs.rationale: Deliberately the least relatable figure in the demo — he exists as pure intellectual threat, capability maxed to justify being the one adversary who can end Holmes.

characters.name: Irene Adler
characters.oneLine: The only person who has ever beaten Sherlock Holmes at his own game — and she did it by being underestimated.
characters.source: Sherlock Holmes canon, Arthur Conan Doyle (public domain)

relationships.note: Outwits his disguise, anticipates his methods, and vanishes with the upper hand — earning a rare, permanent place in his private estimation.
Holds a compromising photograph of the two of them, which the King hires Holmes to retrieve before his royal wedding.

links.note: Her brief, singular appearance defines the thread named for Watson's opening line about her.

arcs.want: To protect herself and her marriage by keeping the photograph as insurance, not blackmail
arcs.need: To be recognized as more than a discarded former mistress
arcs.wound: Being cast off by a king who now fears her existence
arcs.rationale: High capability and proactivity — she out-thinks Holmes in disguise and in strategy — and enough relatability that Watson (and Holmes) end up quietly on her side.

characters.name: The King of Bohemia
characters.role: Hereditary King of Bohemia, travelling incognito
characters.oneLine: A nervous, image-conscious monarch who hires Holmes to retrieve a photograph he fears could wreck his upcoming royal marriage.
characters.source: Sherlock Holmes canon, Arthur Conan Doyle (public domain)

relationships.note: Cast her off once his engagement was arranged, then grew afraid of what she still holds over him.
Hires Holmes to recover the compromising photograph, initially in a thin disguise Holmes sees through at once.

links.note: His fear of exposure is the spark that brings Irene Adler into the story at all.

arcs.want: To recover the photograph before his wedding is announced
arcs.need: To accept that some past entanglements can't simply be paid or ordered away
arcs.wound: A royal position that leaves no room for the life he actually lived
arcs.rationale: A client, not an agent — low across the board on purpose, so the case's real intelligence contest reads as Holmes versus Adler, not Holmes versus the King.

characters.name: Inspector Lestrade
characters.oneLine: A competent, orthodox policeman perpetually one step behind Holmes, who nonetheless keeps coming back to Baker Street when the case gets strange enough.
characters.source: Sherlock Holmes canon, Arthur Conan Doyle (public domain)

relationships.note: Publicly skeptical of Holmes's methods, privately dependent on them.
Treats Watson as a steadier, more reasonable presence than Holmes.

links.note: His home turf and the official face of the law that Holmes routinely outpaces.

arcs.want: To solve the Lauriston Gardens murder before his rival Gregson does
arcs.need: To admit that Holmes's unorthodox methods get results his own can't
arcs.wound: Institutional pride — the Yard's reputation resting on his shoulders
arcs.rationale: Solidly competent, solidly ordinary — the demo needs a baseline the Matrix view can contrast Holmes against.

characters.name: Mycroft Holmes
characters.oneLine: Smarter than Sherlock by his own admission, but too fundamentally indolent to ever leave his armchair at the Diogenes Club and prove it.
characters.source: Sherlock Holmes canon, Arthur Conan Doyle (public domain)

relationships.note: A rare equal, and one of the only people Sherlock defers to intellectually.

links.note: His near-permanent residence; a club built for men who wish to avoid each other's company entirely.

arcs.want: To pass along government-relevant intelligence to Sherlock without leaving his routine
arcs.need: None explored — he is a fixed, stable presence
arcs.wound: None given; his one flaw is a chosen inertia
arcs.rationale: Deliberately near-zero proactivity against maximum capability — the contrast is the entire point of his character.

characters.name: Mrs. Hudson
characters.oneLine: The long-suffering, quietly formidable woman who has kept 221B running through chemical explosions, gunfire indoors, and visitors at three in the morning.
characters.source: Sherlock Holmes canon, Arthur Conan Doyle (public domain)

relationships.note: Tolerates far more than any landlady should, out of equal parts fondness and resignation.
Warmer and more relaxed with Watson than with Holmes, who exhausts her patience regularly.

links.note: She is, functionally, the household's actual foundation.

arcs.want: A quiet, well-run household
arcs.need: Acceptance that quiet was never going to be part of the arrangement
arcs.wound: None specified
arcs.rationale: A grounding, low-key presence — she's here for texture and the relationship web, not for plot-driving.

characters.name: Mary Morstan
characters.oneLine: A composed, self-possessed young woman whose search for her missing father's fortune becomes the case that gives Watson a second chance at happiness.
characters.source: Sherlock Holmes canon, Arthur Conan Doyle (public domain)

relationships.note: He falls for her over the course of the Agra treasure case; they marry shortly after.
Holmes solves her case efficiently and with characteristic detachment from the romance blooming beside him.

links.note: Her missing father and the pearls are the mystery's spine.

arcs.want: To learn what happened to her father and claim the treasure that may be rightfully hers
arcs.need: To let herself trust — and be cared for — after years of a strange, unexplained isolation
arcs.wound: A father who vanished when she was a child, followed by a decade of anonymous pearls with no explanation
arcs.rationale: Warm and sympathetic without needing to out-deduce anyone — her arc resolves through Watson, not through detective work of her own.

characters.name: Jonathan Small
characters.role: Former soldier, convict, the "sign of four" conspirator
characters.oneLine: A one-legged veteran of the Indian Mutiny whose decades-old pact over a stolen treasure finally comes due in London.
characters.source: Sherlock Holmes canon, Arthur Conan Doyle (public domain)

relationships.note: His account, given after capture, finally explains what happened to Captain Morstan and the treasure.
Tracked across London by boat, in one of the canon's most famous chase sequences.

links.note: The origin of the theft and the debt it created.

arcs.want: To reclaim what he sees as his rightful share of the Agra treasure
arcs.need: To reckon with what the pursuit of that treasure has cost — friends, freedom, a leg, decades of his life
arcs.wound: Betrayal by his co-conspirators and a prison sentence that swallowed his best years
arcs.rationale: Given real pathos in his final confession — a villain the reader is allowed, briefly, to understand.

characters.name: Sir Henry Baskerville
characters.oneLine: The last of the Baskerville line, freshly arrived from Canada and unaware that a legendary curse may be about to collect its due on him.
characters.source: Sherlock Holmes canon, Arthur Conan Doyle (public domain)

relationships.note: Under Holmes's protection, largely at a distance, for most of the case.
Watson accompanies him to Dartmoor as guardian and observer while Holmes works unseen.

links.note: His ancestral home and the site of the family curse.
The legend that may or may not be literally true.

arcs.want: To claim his inheritance and settle into a normal life at the Hall
arcs.need: To face the family legend directly instead of living in fear of it
arcs.wound: An inherited dread he doesn't fully believe in but can't quite shake
arcs.rationale: High relatability — an ordinary, likeable man dropped into gothic circumstances — but low capability, since the mystery is solved around him rather than by him.

characters.name: Dr. James Mortimer
characters.role: Country physician, family friend of the Baskervilles
characters.oneLine: The kindly doctor whose walking stick gives Holmes and Watson their first clue — and whose worry over the Baskerville legend sets the whole case in motion.
characters.source: Sherlock Holmes canon, Arthur Conan Doyle (public domain)

relationships.note: Brings the case to Baker Street and provides the crucial manuscript detailing the legend.
Genuinely concerned for Sir Henry's safety, having attended Sir Charles Baskerville at his death.

links.note: His medical practice covers the moor and the Hall.

arcs.want: To protect Sir Henry from whatever killed Sir Charles
arcs.need: To be believed, even though his fears sound superstitious to a man of science
arcs.wound: Having found Sir Charles's body himself, with the hound's footprints beside it
arcs.rationale: A sympathetic, ordinary-competence figure whose worry drives the plot's opening without him ever becoming a central actor.

characters.name: Stapleton
characters.oneLine: An amiable, knowledgeable local naturalist whose easy charm conceals the entire engine of the Baskerville plot.
characters.source: Sherlock Holmes canon, Arthur Conan Doyle (public domain)

relationships.note: Positions himself as a friend while orchestrating events against Sir Henry from the shadows.
Doesn't realize Holmes is on Dartmoor at all until it's too late.

links.note: Uses his intimate knowledge of the Grimpen Mire to stage the hound's appearances.
The human hand behind the "supernatural" legend.

arcs.want: The Baskerville inheritance, which he believes is rightfully his through a hidden family line
arcs.need: None — Doyle gives him no redemptive turn, only unraveling exposure
arcs.wound: A lifetime as an overlooked branch of a wealthy family, left with nothing
arcs.rationale: High proactivity as the case's true engine, but deliberately low relatability — a villain the reader is meant to distrust from early signals, in contrast to Jonathan Small's later sympathy.

worlds.name: Victorian London
worlds.note: Fog, gas lamps, hansom cabs, and a criminal underworld dense enough to need a consulting detective at all.
worlds.source: Sherlock Holmes canon, Arthur Conan Doyle (public domain)

worlds.name: 221B Baker Street
worlds.note: Holmes and Watson's shared lodgings, and the true stage for nearly every case in the canon.
worlds.source: Sherlock Holmes canon, Arthur Conan Doyle (public domain)

worlds.name: Scotland Yard
worlds.note: The official face of London policing, perpetually a half-step behind the amateur genius working out of Baker Street.
worlds.source: Sherlock Holmes canon, Arthur Conan Doyle (public domain)

worlds.name: The Diogenes Club
worlds.note: A gentleman's club built around a single house rule: no member may speak to another, anywhere in the building, except in the visitors' room.
worlds.source: Sherlock Holmes canon, Arthur Conan Doyle (public domain)

worlds.name: Dartmoor / Baskerville Hall
worlds.note: A vast, fog-bound, treacherous moorland in Devon, and the gothic manor at its heart where the Baskerville curse comes home to roost.
worlds.source: Sherlock Holmes canon, Arthur Conan Doyle (public domain)

worlds.name: Reichenbach Falls
worlds.note: A towering waterfall in the Swiss Alps near Meiringen — the site of Holmes and Moriarty's final confrontation.
worlds.source: Sherlock Holmes canon, Arthur Conan Doyle (public domain)

worlds.name: Lauriston Gardens
worlds.note: The site of the empty house where Holmes and Watson's first case together — the Drebber murder — begins.
worlds.source: Sherlock Holmes canon, Arthur Conan Doyle (public domain)

worlds.name: The Agra Fort
worlds.note: A fortress in India where the Agra treasure was originally hidden — the distant origin point of The Sign of Four's central mystery.
worlds.source: Sherlock Holmes canon, Arthur Conan Doyle (public domain)

worlds.name: The Thames / Pool of London
worlds.note: London's working river, and the setting for one of the canon's most famous chase sequences.
worlds.source: Sherlock Holmes canon, Arthur Conan Doyle (public domain)

worlds.name: The Reigate Squire's Estate (Colonel Hayter's)
worlds.note: A minor location, used sparingly for flavor — a rural retreat where Holmes recuperates between cases.
worlds.source: Sherlock Holmes canon, Arthur Conan Doyle (public domain)

timeline.label: A doctor and a stranger split the rent
timeline.summary: Invalided out of the army, Dr. John Watson is introduced by a mutual acquaintance to a strange, brilliant man looking to share lodgings at 221B Baker Street. Holmes deduces Watson's entire military history from a handshake.

timeline.label: RACHE at Lauriston Gardens
timeline.summary: A body is found in an empty house on Lauriston Gardens with no wound and the word RACHE written in blood on the wall. Holmes reads the entire scene — and the murderer's cab, gait, and cigar — before Lestrade's men have finished their notes.

timeline.label: The chase and the confession
timeline.summary: Holmes traps the murderer, a cab driver named Jefferson Hope, whose confession reveals a decades-old revenge story that began in the American West and ends, finally, in a London sitting room.

timeline.label: A ring, a pearl, and a summons
timeline.summary: Mary Morstan brings Holmes and Watson a strange case: a decade of anonymous pearls sent to her every year, and now a summons to recover a treasure connected to her long-vanished father.

timeline.label: The wooden-legged man and the Aurora
timeline.summary: The trail leads to Jonathan Small, a wooden-legged former convict, and a thrilling launch chase down the Thames as he tries to flee aboard his boat, the Aurora, with the recovered treasure.

timeline.label: Watson proposes
timeline.summary: With the case resolved, Watson asks Mary Morstan to marry him — the beginning of the domestic life that will quietly reshape his friendship with Holmes.

timeline.label: A Scandal in Bohemia — "the woman"
timeline.summary: The King of Bohemia hires Holmes to recover a compromising photograph from his former lover, Irene Adler — who outmaneuvers Holmes's disguise, anticipates his methods, and vanishes with the upper hand, becoming the only person ever to best him.

timeline.label: The Red-Headed League
timeline.summary: A pawnbroker's absurd part-time job copying the Encyclopedia Britannica by hand turns out to be cover for a bank vault tunnel — one of Holmes's most purely delightful deductions.

timeline.label: Silver Blaze and the dog that didn't bark
timeline.summary: A champion racehorse vanishes and its trainer is found dead. Holmes solves it by noticing what didn't happen — the stable dog's silence during the theft — rather than what did.

timeline.label: The Napoleon of crime, named
timeline.summary: Holmes tells Watson, for the first time, of Professor Moriarty — the criminal mastermind behind half the undetected crime in London, and the one mind Holmes has ever met that equals his own.

timeline.label: Flight to the Continent
timeline.summary: With Moriarty's agents closing in, Holmes and Watson flee London together across Europe, evading assassination attempts and narrowing, at last, toward Switzerland.

timeline.label: The Reichenbach Falls
timeline.summary: Lured away by a false errand, Watson returns to the falls to find only Holmes's note and two sets of footprints leading to the ledge, none leading away. Holmes and Moriarty, it seems, have gone over together.

timeline.label: Watson writes the elegy
timeline.summary: Watson closes the Memoirs believing his closest friend is dead, writing what he intends as a final, honest account of the best and wisest man he has ever known.

timeline.label: Dr. Mortimer's stick
timeline.summary: A country doctor leaves his walking stick behind at Baker Street, giving Holmes and Watson the chance to reconstruct his entire history before he returns — and to hear the legend of the Baskerville hound for the first time.

timeline.label: Sir Henry arrives, and is followed
timeline.summary: The new heir to Baskerville Hall arrives in London and is immediately shadowed by a mysterious bearded stranger — while a threatening note assembled from cut newspaper letters warns him off the moor entirely.

timeline.label: Watson alone on Dartmoor
timeline.summary: Holmes sends Watson ahead to Baskerville Hall alone to guard Sir Henry and gather intelligence, testing how far the partnership's trust can stretch without Holmes physically present.

timeline.label: The man on the tor
timeline.summary: Watson discovers a mysterious figure has been secretly living in a stone hut on the moor, watching events unfold — and it turns out to be Holmes himself, who never left for London at all.

timeline.label: The hound in the fog
timeline.summary: Sir Henry is lured across the moor at night and pursued by a genuinely terrifying hound — painted with phosphorescent paint to look spectral — before Holmes and Watson shoot it down and expose Stapleton's scheme to claim the inheritance himself.

chapters.title: A Scandal in Bohemia
chapters.summary: Watson visits Holmes after his marriage and finds him newly absorbed in a case for the King of Bohemia — recovering a compromising photograph from Irene Adler, a woman who will prove more than Holmes bargained for.

chapters.title: Mr. Sherlock Holmes
chapters.summary: Watson examines a walking stick left behind by a mysterious visitor and attempts, with mixed success, to deduce its owner's history using Holmes's own methods — setting up the arrival of Dr. Mortimer and the legend of the hound.

notes.text: New lodger at 221B has an unnerving habit of announcing facts about strangers before they've spoken a word. Query: chemistry, boxing, singlestick — catalogue his skills properly before I forget half of them.
Miss Morstan's pearls — six sent so far, always the finest quality, no note, no name. If this is guilt money, whoever sends it has a great deal to feel guilty about.
Holmes asked for "the woman's" photograph as his fee instead of the emerald ring offered. First time I've seen him keep a memento of a case rather than simply close the file on it.
Received Holmes's note from Meiringen. Reading it again — and again — hoping I've misunderstood something in it. I have not.

Sir Charles found dead in the yew alley, face reportedly altered by terror. Mortimer swears there were footprints beside the body — of an enormous hound. I do not believe in curses. I am trying very hard not to believe in this one either.
Someone has been living in a stone hut on the tor for days — food brought in, a boy running messages. Whoever it is knows this moor far better than a stranger has any right to.

themes.name: Reason versus intuition
themes.statement: Even the most disciplined intellect cannot fully account for what it refuses to feel.

themes.name: Loyalty as the true detective work
themes.statement: The partnership between Holmes and Watson solves as much as the deductions do.

themes.name: The mask that outsmarts the observer
themes.statement: The most dangerous opponent is the one who understands they're being watched and plans for it.

themes.name: Old debts always come due
themes.statement: The past — a betrayal, a theft, a wound from another continent — never stays buried; it simply waits for a case to surface it in.

themes.name: The cost of being irreplaceable
themes.statement: To be the only person who can solve a problem is to become the only person an enemy needs to remove.

reading.title: The Murders in the Rue Morgue, The Purloined Letter, The Mystery of Marie Rogêt
reading.author: Edgar Allan Poe
reading.gives: The genre's origin grammar — the eccentric genius detective, the less-brilliant narrator-companion, and the solve-then-explain reveal structure, invented in three short stories in the 1840s.
reading.correlation: Poe shows the solution first, then rewinds to show how the detective got there, clue by clue — still the dominant reveal shape in the genre today. Read for structure, not for prose style; his sentences are dense and formal by modern standards.
takeaways: Borrow the solve-then-explain reveal shape
Study the narrator-companion relationship in embryo, before Doyle perfected it

reading.title: The Complete Sherlock Holmes canon
reading.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
reading.gives: The Holmes/Watson dynamic — the genre's most influential relationship — plus the case-of-the-week structure and deduction-as-showmanship set pieces.
reading.correlation: A narrator-companion of ordinary intelligence is almost always a better viewpoint character than the detective. The reader feels smart watching Watson be astonished, even while staying behind Holmes. Give your detective a signature method and let the reader learn to anticipate it, the way they'd learn a magician's style.
takeaways: Borrow the Watson device — a companion narrator of ordinary intelligence
Give the detective a signature method as recurring showmanship
Watch for fair-play looseness — Holmes sometimes knows things the reader had no way to deduce; decide early whether your detective plays strictly fair or not

reading.title: The Moonstone; The Woman in White
reading.author: Wilkie Collins
reading.gives: Often called the first true detective novel. Multiple narrators telling the same events from different angles, the truth assembled by the reader from the gaps between accounts.
reading.correlation: The multi-narrator structure is a powerful tool if your book has more than one investigator, or if you want the reader to distrust any single account — it solves the problem of a mystery too large for one Watson to witness firsthand.
takeaways: Borrow the multi-narrator, partial-account structure for mysteries too big for one witness
Watch for Victorian pacing — patient in a way that reads slow to modern readers; study the structure more than the sentence rhythm

reading.title: The Murder of Roger Ackroyd; And Then There Were None; Murder on the Orient Express
reading.author: Agatha Christie
reading.gives: The fair-play contract formalized — every clue the detective uses is shown to the reader in plain sight before the reveal. The closed-circle suspect pool. The honest red herring.
reading.correlation: If a detective story should feel like a puzzle the reader can play along with, Christie is the master class. Every suspect needs a motive, an opportunity, and a false reason to seem guilty. Plant the real clue early and bury it under three false ones of equal visual weight.
takeaways: Borrow the fair-play contract — show every clue the detective ultimately uses
Borrow honest red herrings and the closed-circle suspect pool
Watch for flattened character — Christie's suspects are sometimes types more than people; pair her clue-fairness with real interiority if the book wants deep characters

reading.title: The Big Sleep; The Long Goodbye; "The Simple Art of Murder" (essay)
reading.author: Raymond Chandler
reading.gives: The hardboiled detective as a morally exhausted man moving through a corrupt world he can't fix, only survive. Voice-driven first-person narration where the similes do as much work as the plot.
reading.correlation: If the book wants moral weight — a detective changed or worn down by what they investigate, rather than one who solves and moves on unbothered — Chandler is the model. Worth reading directly against Doyle: Watson is warm and admiring, Marlowe is guarded and worn.
takeaways: Borrow the dry, metaphor-rich hardboiled first-person voice
Borrow the case-as-tour-of-a-broken-social-landscape approach
Watch for plot looseness — a deliberate stylistic choice for Chandler, not something to imitate by accident, especially if readers expect fair-play clues

reading.title: Gaudy Night; Strong Poison; the Lord Peter Wimsey series
reading.author: Dorothy L. Sayers
reading.gives: A detective allowed to fall in love, doubt himself, and change over the course of a series — genuine long-arc character development inside a genre that mostly kept its detectives static.
reading.correlation: The strongest classic-canon model for a detective with a real multi-book arc — want/need/wound, evolving relatability — without losing the puzzle-plot machinery.
takeaways: Borrow the technique for letting a detective actually grow across a series
Study how literary-ambition prose can sit comfortably inside genre plotting

reading.title: The Innocence of Father Brown
reading.author: G.K. Chesterton
reading.gives: A detective whose method is psychological and moral insight rather than physical-clue deduction — Father Brown reasons from what kind of person could or couldn't do a given thing.
reading.correlation: A genuinely different detective archetype from Holmes's "reasoning machine" — foundational and older than the modern profiler archetype, useful if the detective's gift is reading people rather than physical evidence.
takeaways: Borrow a reasoning-from-human-nature method as an alternative to physical-clue deduction

reading.title: The Name of the Rose
reading.author: Umberto Eco
reading.gives: A murder mystery set in a medieval monastery, built explicitly as a tribute to Holmes — the detective-monk William of Baskerville is a direct homage.
reading.correlation: Useful for seeing how a mystery structure can carry enormous worldbuilding and thematic weight without losing its puzzle spine — directly relevant when a detective story is also doing heavy worldbuilding.
takeaways: Study how the puzzle spine supports heavy thematic and world weight without collapsing

reading.title: When We Were Orphans
reading.author: Kazuo Ishiguro
reading.gives: A literary novel that uses detective-story structure and imagery while subverting the genre's promise of a clean, satisfying solution.
reading.correlation: Useful for studying unreliable narration and how a mystery's emotional resolution can matter more than its factual one.
takeaways: Study a mystery that resolves the character before it resolves the case

reading.title: In the Woods (Dublin Murder Squad series)
reading.author: Tana French
reading.gives: Modern police-procedural craft with real literary prose — forensic and procedural realism balanced against deep character interiority.
reading.correlation: Updates the Sayers project — a detective with a real inner life — for a modern procedural context.
takeaways: Study the balance of forensic detail against a detective's inner life

reading.title: The Daughter of Time
reading.author: Josephine Tey
reading.gives: A detective solves a five-hundred-year-old cold case from a hospital bed using only historical documents — pure deductive reasoning as narrative engine, almost no physical action.
reading.correlation: Useful for scenes where a detective reasons aloud with a companion and the reasoning itself is the drama — closer to Doyle's deduction set pieces than to modern thriller pacing.
takeaways: Study scenes where reasoning itself, not physical action, carries the tension

prose.a-scandal-in-bohemia:
# A Scandal in Bohemia

To Sherlock Holmes she is always _the_ woman. I have seldom heard him mention her under any other name. In his eyes she eclipses and predominates the whole of her sex. It was not that he felt any emotion akin to love for Irene Adler. All emotions, and that one particularly, were abhorrent to his cold, precise but admirably balanced mind. He was, I take it, the most perfect reasoning and observing machine that the world has seen, but as a lover he would have placed himself in a false position. He never spoke of the softer passions, save with a gibe and a sneer. They were admirable things for the observer—excellent for drawing the veil from men's motives and actions. But for the trained reasoner to admit such intrusions into his own delicate and finely adjusted temperament was to introduce a distracting factor which might throw a doubt upon all his mental results. Grit in a sensitive instrument, or a crack in one of his own high-power lenses, would not be more disturbing than a strong emotion in a nature such as his. And yet there was but one woman to him, and that woman was the late Irene Adler, of dubious and questionable memory.

I had seen little of Holmes lately. My marriage had drifted us away from each other. My own complete happiness, and the home-centred interests which rise up around the man who first finds himself master of his own establishment, were sufficient to absorb all my attention, while Holmes, who loathed every form of society with his whole Bohemian soul, remained in our lodgings in Baker Street, buried among his old books, and alternating from week to week between cocaine and ambition, the drowsiness of the drug, and the fierce energy of his own keen nature. He was still, as ever, deeply attracted by the study of crime, and occupied his immense faculties and extraordinary powers of observation in following out those clues, and clearing up those mysteries which had been abandoned as hopeless by the official police. From time to time I heard some vague account of his doings: of his summons to Odessa in the case of the Trepoff murder, of his clearing up of the singular tragedy of the Atkinson brothers at Trincomalee, and finally of the mission which he had accomplished so delicately and successfully for the reigning family of Holland. Beyond these signs of his activity, however, which I merely shared with all the readers of the daily press, I knew little of my former friend and companion.

One night—it was on the twentieth of March, 1888—I was returning from a journey to a patient (for I had now returned to civil practice), when my way led me through Baker Street. As I passed the well-remembered door, which must always be associated in my mind with my wooing, and with the dark incidents of the Study in Scarlet, I was seized with a keen desire to see Holmes again, and to know how he was employing his extraordinary powers. His rooms were brilliantly lit, and, even as I looked up, I saw his tall, spare figure pass twice in a dark silhouette against the blind. He was pacing the room swiftly, eagerly, with his head sunk upon his chest and his hands clasped behind him. To me, who knew his every mood and habit, his attitude and manner told their own story. He was at work again. He had risen out of his drug-created dreams and was hot upon the scent of some new problem. I rang the bell and was shown up to the chamber which had formerly been in part my own.

His manner was not effusive. It seldom was; but he was glad, I think, to see me. With hardly a word spoken, but with a kindly eye, he waved me to an armchair, threw across his case of cigars, and indicated a spirit case and a gasogene in the corner. Then he stood before the fire and looked me over in his singular introspective fashion.

"Wedlock suits you," he remarked. "I think, Watson, that you have put on seven and a half pounds since I saw you."

"Seven!" I answered.

"Indeed, I should have thought a little more. Just a trifle more, I fancy, Watson. And in practice again, I observe. You did not tell me that you intended to go into harness."

"Then, how do you know?"

"I see it, I deduce it. How do I know that you have been getting yourself very wet lately, and that you have a most clumsy and careless servant girl?"

"My dear Holmes," said I, "this is too much. You would certainly have been burned, had you lived a few centuries ago. It is true that I had a country walk on Thursday and came home in a dreadful mess, but as I have changed my clothes I can't imagine how you deduce it. As to Mary Jane, she is incorrigible, and my wife has given her notice, but there, again, I fail to see how you work it out."

He chuckled to himself and rubbed his long, nervous hands together.

"It is simplicity itself," said he; "my eyes tell me that on the inside of your left shoe, just where the firelight strikes it, the leather is scored by six almost parallel cuts. Obviously they have been caused by someone who has very carelessly scraped round the edges of the sole in order to remove crusted mud from it. Hence, you see, my double deduction that you had been out in vile weather, and that you had a particularly malignant boot-slitting specimen of the London slavey. As to your practice, if a gentleman walks into my rooms smelling of iodoform, with a black mark of nitrate of silver upon his right forefinger, and a bulge on the right side of his top-hat to show where he has secreted his stethoscope, I must be dull, indeed, if I do not pronounce him to be an active member of the medical profession."

I could not help laughing at the ease with which he explained his process of deduction. "When I hear you give your reasons," I remarked, "the thing always appears to me to be so ridiculously simple that I could easily do it myself, though at each successive instance of your reasoning I am baffled until you explain your process. And yet I believe that my eyes are as good as yours."

---

*Source: Project Gutenberg, "The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes" by Arthur Conan Doyle (eBook #1661), https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/1661/pg1661.txt — public domain.*
prose.mr-sherlock-holmes:
# Mr. Sherlock Holmes

Mr. Sherlock Holmes, who was usually very late in the mornings, save upon those not infrequent occasions when he was up all night, was seated at the breakfast table.

I stood upon the hearth-rug and picked up the stick which our visitor had left behind him the night before. It was a fine, thick piece of wood, bulbous-headed, of the sort which is known as a "Penang lawyer." Just under the head was a broad silver band nearly an inch across. "To James Mortimer, M.R.C.S., from his friends of the C.C.H.," was engraved upon it, with the date "1884." It was just such a stick as the old-fashioned family practitioner used to carry—dignified, solid, and reassuring.

"Well, Watson, what do you make of it?"

Holmes was sitting with his back to me, and I had given him no sign of my occupation.

"How did you know what I was doing? I believe you have eyes in the back of your head."

"I have, at least, a well-polished, silver-plated coffee-pot in front of me," said he. "But, tell me, Watson, what do you make of our visitor's stick? Since we have been so unfortunate as to miss him and have no notion of his errand, this accidental souvenir becomes of importance. Let me hear you reconstruct the man by an examination of it."

"I think," said I, following as far as I could the methods of my companion, "that Dr. Mortimer is a successful, elderly medical man, well-esteemed since those who know him give him this mark of their appreciation."

"Good!" said Holmes. "Excellent!"

"I think also that the probability is in favour of his being a country practitioner who does a great deal of his visiting on foot."

"Why so?"

"Because this stick, though originally a very handsome one has been so knocked about that I can hardly imagine a town practitioner carrying it. The thick-iron ferrule is worn down, so it is evident that he has done a great amount of walking with it."

"Perfectly sound!" said Holmes.

"And then again, there is the 'friends of the C.C.H.' I should guess that to be the Something Hunt, the local hunt to whose members he has possibly given some surgical assistance, and which has made him a small presentation in return."

"Really, Watson, you excel yourself," said Holmes, pushing back his chair and lighting a cigarette.

---

*Source: Project Gutenberg, "The Hound of the Baskervilles" by Arthur Conan Doyle (eBook #2852), https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/2852/pg2852.txt — public domain.*

worldbuilding.victorian-london: London in the 1880s and 1890s is a city of extremes — the same square mile holds Mycroft's gentleman's clubs and the opium dens of the docks, Scotland Yard's new detective bureau and the rookeries the police won't enter without an escort. Gas lamps make islands of light in a fog that can swallow a hansom cab whole; the Underground is young and half-finished; telegrams move faster than any person can. It's a city built, almost deliberately, for someone like Holmes: dense enough to hide anything, orderly enough on the surface that any real deviation stands out to a mind trained to see it. Watson's London is comfortable and a little weary — a doctor's-eye view of a city that never quite sleeps and never quite tells you everything at once.
worldbuilding.221b-baker-street: Two rooms up a narrow flight of seventeen steps from Mrs. Hudson's front hall: a shared sitting room and separate bedrooms. The sitting room is a study in productive chaos — a chemistry corner with acid-stained deal-topped tables, a mantelpiece where Holmes keeps his unanswered correspondence pinned with a jackknife, a Persian slipper stuffed with tobacco, and a coal-scuttle that (in later stories) holds his cigars. Bullet holes from an indoor bout of target practice mark a patriotic "VR" into the wallpaper. Books are piled by subject rather than shelved — Holmes's index of criminal cases and his monographs on cigar ash and tattoo marks share space with Watson's medical texts. The bow window looks down on Baker Street itself, useful for watching a client's cab arrive and reading their entire recent history before they've reached the door. It is, depending on the week, a laboratory, a shooting range, a case-file archive, and — for Watson especially — the only place that has ever felt fully like home.
worldbuilding.scotland-yard: Scotland Yard represents order, procedure, and institutional caution — everything Holmes's method deliberately isn't. Its detectives, Lestrade chief among them, are neither fools nor villains; they're competent professionals working within rules, paperwork, and public accountability that Holmes simply ignores. The Yard needs Holmes precisely because it can't afford to operate the way he does — and resents needing him for exactly the same reason. Every case that reaches Baker Street through Scotland Yard's door is, structurally, an admission that the official method has already failed.
worldbuilding.the-diogenes-club: Mycroft Holmes's natural habitat. The Diogenes Club exists for men who find other men's company tiring but still want somewhere comfortable to sit in it — silence is enforced, and a third infraction means expulsion. It is the perfect architecture for Mycroft: a place built to accommodate a towering intellect that simply cannot be bothered to exert itself socially, or often at all. Sherlock's visits here are rare and always mean the matter is serious enough to move his brother out of his armchair.
worldbuilding.dartmoor-baskerville-hall: Dartmoor is Holmes's London turned inside out — instead of dense streets and gaslight, it's open, empty, and dangerous precisely because there's nowhere to hide except the ground itself swallows you. The Grimpen Mire is the moor's most feared feature: a bog that can pull a misstepping pony under in minutes, marked by paths only a local — like Stapleton — could know well enough to cross safely. Baskerville Hall itself is a dark, ivy-choked manor with a yew alley where Sir Charles met his death, mullioned windows, and a family portrait gallery Holmes studies for a very particular reason. An escaped convict loose on the moor, ancient legend, isolated tenant farms, and a spectral hound heard howling in the fog make Dartmoor feel like a different genre entirely — Doyle deliberately writes it as gothic horror before Holmes's reasoning drags it back into the world of the explicable.
worldbuilding.reichenbach-falls: A narrow path along the gorge, cut into the rock, leading to a viewing point where the water's roar makes conversation nearly impossible and a single misstep means the end. Doyle chose it as deliberately as any writer choosing a stage for a duel — remote enough that no rescue is plausible, dramatic enough that a fall reads as final. Watson's account has him lured away by a false errand, arriving back to find only two sets of footprints leading to the ledge and none leading away — and Holmes's note, left behind, explaining what he believes is about to happen. Whatever really occurred there, the falls become the single most consequential location in the entire canon.
worldbuilding.lauriston-gardens: A dingy, half-suburban stretch off the Brixton Road with a handful of houses standing empty for lack of tenants. The scene of the crime that opens A Study in Scarlet: a locked, unfurnished house, a corpse with no visible wound, and the word RACHE written in blood on the wall. It's Holmes's first true showcase to Watson — and to the reader — of deduction performed on a genuinely blank scene, with almost nothing to go on but what everyone else has already dismissed as unremarkable.
worldbuilding.the-agra-fort: Referenced rather than visited on the page: the fort where, during the chaos of the Indian Mutiny, a fortune in jewels was hidden and then fought over by the men who found it — a debt and a betrayal that follows its survivors all the way back to London decades later. It functions as the mystery's origin myth, the distant "before" that explains everything happening in the present-day case.
worldbuilding.the-thames-pool-of-london: Crowded with barges, steam launches, and cargo traffic, the Thames through the Pool of London is as much a highway as any street — and one Holmes uses to devastating effect when he commandeers a police launch to run down Jonathan Small's boat, the Aurora, in a chase through fog and river traffic that closes out The Sign of Four's central mystery.
worldbuilding.a-study-in-scarlet: A discharged army doctor named John Watson, searching for cheap lodgings, is introduced to an eccentric stranger who can deduce a man's entire history from a glance. Their first case together — a murder with the word RACHE scrawled in blood — reveals just how far Sherlock Holmes's methods can reach, and how far one man's grievance can travel across an ocean and half a lifetime to collect its due.
worldbuilding.the-sign-of-four: A young woman receives a mysterious pearl every year from an anonymous benefactor, then an invitation to recover a vanished treasure. Holmes and Watson are pulled into a story of stolen Agra treasure, a wooden-legged killer, and a debt of blood from the Indian Mutiny — while Watson finds himself falling for the client he's meant to be protecting.
worldbuilding.the-adventures-of-sherlock-holmes: Twelve short cases, newly married Watson's first collection of Holmes's exploits for the public. Includes "A Scandal in Bohemia," in which Holmes meets the only person ever to outwit him — and loses, gracefully, for the first time.
worldbuilding.the-memoirs-of-sherlock-holmes: A darker, more introspective set of cases, culminating in "The Final Problem" — Watson's account of Holmes's collision with Professor Moriarty, the "Napoleon of crime," and their shared plunge over the Reichenbach Falls. The book that was meant to end the series.
worldbuilding.the-hound-of-the-baskervilles: A family curse, a spectral hound, and a death on the moor bring Holmes back from apparent retirement (in the story's internal chronology, a case predating Reichenbach) to protect the last heir of Baskerville Hall from a beast that may not be entirely supernatural — or entirely animal.
